bearings.paper_claim: The authors argue that comparing points before and after a coach-called timeout is fallacious because coaches often call timeouts to stop momentum. They use TV timeouts, which fall at predetermined times, and match runs interrupted by a TV timeout to uninterrupted runs on propensity scores (pairs; unmatched runs dropped). Result: -11.2% points over the next 3 minutes (b = -0.119, SE 0.012), n = 5,148 matched runs. Caveat from the same paper: Appendix E (as described in the main text) finds coaches' timeouts give largely similar, slightly larger effects, and the TV-vs-coach coefficient difference was not significant; Sec. 5.3 concedes TV timeouts may not be fully exogenous.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 1 p.118 (text lines 81-86); Sec. 2 p.119-120; Sec. 4 p.122-123 (propensity matching); Table 3 p.125; Sec. 5.2 p.129 (Appendix E summary); Sec. 5.3
bearings.system_side: H2 scores frozen pressure_mult against |overall-tier movement| with an unadjusted cross-sectional Spearman. PROTOCOL_TEXT plans an engaged-only run among members the In-contact log marks engaged, but states it is unavailable until separately specified, receipted contact data exists; the result field is engaged_only = NOT_IMPLEMENTED_NO_CONTACT_CONTRACT. CLAIM_SCOPE = receptivity_forecast_only_not_spending_effects.

bearings.transfer_conditions: Design logic only, not effect size. Lobbyist-chosen contact is endogenous like a coach's timeout, so an engaged-only rho would confound pressure_mult with targeting unless contact timing is exogenous or matched on targeting covariates. The engaged-only arm is a subgroup correlation, not a before/after-contact comparison, so the analogy is to the selection problem, not an identical design. The paper's own Appendix E finding (coach vs TV timeouts not significantly different) means it does not empirically show the endogenous design is badly biased in its setting. Single observational study with matching.

bearings.paper_claim: A Monte Carlo with zero true momentum (130,000 independent 50/50 scoring plays, a TV timeout after one play in every 50, substitutions not simulated) yields a null treatment coefficient (b = 0.002, SE 0.022, n = 1,336). The Fig. 6 caption calls it a negative control showing the matched design does not find an effect where none exists.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 5.2 p.127-128; Table 5 p.128; Fig. 6 caption
bearings.system_side: The discipline already used a simulated null to calibrate its protocol: a joint-null false-pass simulation (pass-both-panels about 1.5-2%, dual dominance under 1%) supported exactly one more look per trait.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Supports the general practice of simulating under a known null to check that a selection or gating rule cannot manufacture a pass. Says nothing about the 1.5-2% figure or pre-registration; the brain simulation concerns look false-pass rates, not engine outcome estimators.
bearings.verifier_note: Table 5 values and Fig. 6 negative-control wording confirmed in text; brain note line 56 confirmed.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper's Monte Carlo is a negative control for an estimator applied to observed data: simulate data with no effect, re-run the matching estimator, expect a null.
bearings.system_side: scenario.py uses Monte Carlo as a forward model: baseline vs scenario competitive-cascade spread under edge-keyed common random numbers (SEED=7, MC default 40), so an unperturbed scenario gives a zero delta by construction. That is an identity property of the simulator, not a negative control on an inferred effect.

bearings.transfer_conditions: A Weimer-style placebo applies to empirical estimators that read observed outcomes (forecasters, the contract), not to the forward cascade's deltas, which are model outputs.

bearings.paper_claim: Appendix D (described in the main text) re-tallies post-treatment points over windows from 60 s to 4 minutes in 10 s steps; the negative effect persists but the point estimate steadily decreases as the window lengthens, and there is no significant effect for points scored between minutes 3 and 4. The first-minute effect is about four times the 3-minute effect.

bearings.system_side: mc_stability_check.py reruns one topic's budget frontier at MC=20/100 and SEED=7/1/13 and reports Jaccard set overlap; receptivity_sensitivity.py sweeps receptivity constants and labels ROBUST when top-20 overlap >= 18. The outcome contract has no window sweep: the window is whatever elapses between freeze and score, with a 60-day minimum and 150 movers before it stops returning UNDERPOWERED.

related.why: Imai & Kim recast two-way fixed effects as a matching estimator and show its causal limits; Weimer uses matching on a natural experiment. Both bear on reading observational looks causally.

Blackwell & Yamauchi adjust for unmeasured confounding of strategically placed interest-group ads; Weimer concedes unmeasured strategy changes during timeouts as a limitation. Same strategic-treatment confounding problem.
Kalla & Broockman randomize which congressional offices receive a donor-identified meeting request: the randomized ideal of Weimer's Table 1, in the political-contact domain.

Harrison is a general Monte Carlo tutorial that runs no simulation itself; Weimer applies Monte Carlo as a negative control. Background reference, not the same method application (relation changed from same-method).

summary_issues: 'The effect is larger for longer runs (n = 576 and 48)' overstates: for runs >= 10 (n = 576) the effect is 11.57% vs 11.2% for runs >= 6, essentially the same; only runs >= 15 (n = 48) show a larger effect (30.79%), which the authors say to interpret cautiously given the small n.

The summary omits that Appendix E (per main text p.129) finds coaches' timeouts give largely similar, slightly larger effects and the TV-vs-coach difference was not significant, and that Sec. 5.3 concedes TV timeouts may not be fully exogenous. 'Coach timeouts bias the comparison' is the authors' design argument, not a bias they demonstrated in their data.

'The contact-conditioned arm it plans is exactly the coach-timeout design' overstates: the engaged-only arm is a subgroup Spearman among contacted members, not a before/after-contact comparison, and PROTOCOL_TEXT already says it is unavailable until separately specified contact data exists. The shared issue is selection on a chosen treatment, not an identical design.
Minor: '1:1 on propensity scores' is a fair paraphrase (each treated run matched to a maximally similar control, pairs kept), but the paper does not use the term 1:1.

The 'no negative control in fec/engine' claim holds for fec/engine (no placebo / negative control / null simulation hits); negative controls exist in fec/tests/run_tests.py but are code-test controls, not estimator placebos. Keep the claim scoped to fec/engine and UNVERIFIED under DE-062.
